With db_superuser the daemon even succeeds in CREATE DATABASE dify_plugin and still cannot connect to it, so the database exists and the container crash-loops on exit 2 anyway. Set the daemon's DB_DATABASE to ${PGDATABASE} (NOT ${DB_PLUGIN_DATABASE}). Verified safe on 1.16.1: the api creates 136 tables and the daemon's 13 (plugins, plugin_installations, plugin_declarations, endpoints, serverless_runtimes, datasource_installations, tool_installations, ai_model_installations, install_tasks, tenant_storages, agent_strategy_installations, trigger_installations, plugin_readme_records) collide with none of them. Everything else in the stack comes up green while this one crash-loops, so the console looks fine and plugins are simply dead: check `docker ps` for plugin_daemon, do not trust the access point."
  - "1.16.1 IS 15 CONTAINERS, NOT NINE. The release added a Dify Agent tier (agent_backend + local_sandbox + agent_ssrf_proxy) and a dedicated api_websocket. Full keep-list: init_permissions, api, api_websocket, worker, worker_beat, web, nginx, redis, sandbox, local_sandbox, plugin_daemon, agent_backend, ssrf_proxy, agent_ssrf_proxy, weaviate. Measured idle footprint on m1.mem16: 2.7 GB of 16 GB used. m1.mem16 remains right; m1.large (8 GB) would survive idle and is a real risk under dataset indexing."
  - "MOST OF THE COMPOSE IS BEHIND `profiles:` IN 1.16.x, AND .env.example SETS COMPOSE_PROFILES=${VECTOR_STORE:-weaviate},${DB_TYPE:-postgresql},collaboration. Do not rely on the compose engine honouring profiles. DELETE the services you do not want outright and STRIP `profiles:` from the ones you keep (weaviate, api_websocket), then set COMPOSE_PROFILES= empty. Leave the postgresql profile enabled by accident and you get the second Postgres this file already warns about; leave weaviate gated and the vector store never starts at all."
  - "THE `envs/` env_file ENTRIES ARE NO-OPS. Every service lists ~25 `env_file: - path: ./envs/... required: false` entries, but the repo ships only *.env.example under docker/envs/ — the real files do not exist. Collapse each service's env_file to `- ./.env` and the stack behaves identically with 75 fewer lines. Keeping them costs nothing on docker but is one more thing podman can trip on."
  - "DECLARE THE `default` NETWORK EXPLICITLY. Services name `default` in their networks: list but upstream never defines it, and podman-compose refuses the whole file with `RuntimeError: missing networks: default`. Adding `default: {driver: bridge}` to the networks block fixes it and is a no-op under docker. Worth doing even if you pass compose_engine:'docker', so the file stays portable."
  - "PREFER compose_engine:'docker' FOR THIS STACK. It uses modern compose-spec that podman-compose 1.0.6 handles poorly (env_file long-form, depends_on conditions incl. service_completed_successfully), and nginx's /socket.io/ block hardcodes `resolver [ip]`, which is DOCKER's embedded DNS — under podman that location cannot resolve and workflow collaboration breaks while the rest of the console looks fine. Confirmed working: deploy_compose with compose_engine:'docker' on 1.16.1."
  - "USE NAMED VOLUMES, NOT THE ./volumes BIND MOUNTS, FOR DURABLE STATE. Upstream binds ./volumes/app/storage, ./volumes/plugin_daemon, ./volumes/weaviate and ./volumes/redis/data inside the project directory, which is exactly what a source re-upload replaces. Move those four to named volumes (app_storage, plugin_storage, weaviate_data, redis_data). Bonus: a fresh named volume inherits /app/api/storage's uid 1001 ownership from the image, so the init_permissions chown becomes belt-and-braces instead of load-bearing. Keep ./volumes/sandbox/conf, ./nginx and ./ssrf_proxy as bind mounts — those are config shipped in the tarball."
  - "SET MORE THAN FIVE URL VARIABLES ON 1.16.x. Beyond the five above, these also default to empty or to localhost and are wrong behind a real hostname: FILES_URL (file previews and multimodal), TRIGGER_URL, ENDPOINT_URL_TEMPLATE (https://<host>/e/{hook_id}), and NEXT_PUBLIC_SOCKET_URL, which ships as ws://localhost and must become wss://<host> or the collaboration websocket fails against a TLS origin. Set INTERNAL_FILES_URL=http://api:5001 too. Good check after deploy: `curl -s https://<host>/install | grep -c localhost:5001` must be 0."
  - "CAP THE SQLALCHEMY POOL. .env.example ships SQLALCHEMY_POOL_SIZE=30 with MAX_OVERFLOW=10, and api + api_websocket + worker + worker_beat each open their own pool: up to 160 connections against a managed m1.small Postgres whose max_connections you do not control. Drop to SQLALCHEMY_POOL_SIZE=10 / SQLALCHEMY_MAX_OVERFLOW=5 and set SQLALCHEMY_POOL_PRE_PING=true."
  - "SET MIGRATION_ENABLED=false ON worker, worker_beat AND api_websocket. The image entrypoint runs `flask upgrade-db` whenever the variable is true, regardless of MODE, so all four containers race the same migration on a fresh database. Leave it true only on api. The others crash-loop briefly until the tables exist, then settle — restart: always covers it."
  - "MORE CREDENTIALS THAN THE FILE USED TO SAY. 1.16.1 ships well-known defaults for SANDBOX_API_KEY/CODE_EXECUTION_API_KEY (must match each other), PLUGIN_DAEMON_KEY, PLUGIN_DIFY_INNER_API_KEY, WEAVIATE_API_KEY (must match WEAVIATE_AUTHENTICATION_APIKEY_ALLOWED_KEYS), DIFY_AGENT_API_TOKEN, DIFY_AGENT_SERVER_SECRET_KEY and an EMPTY DIFY_AGENT_SHELLCTL_AUTH_TOKEN. Regenerate all of them. Also flip WEAVIATE_AUTHENTICATION_ANONYMOUS_ACCESS_ENABLED to false — .env.example sets it true even though the compose default is false."
  - "SECRET_KEY IS NO LONGER STRICTLY REQUIRED BUT STILL SET IT. 1.16.1's .env.example comments that an empty value auto-generates a persistent key into the storage directory. That key then lives only in the storage volume, so losing the volume logs everyone out. Passing your own value keeps it in your hands and in the redeploy recipe."
  - "DROP nginx's 443 PUBLISH AND plugin_daemon's 5003 PUBLISH. Upstream publishes ${EXPOSE_NGINX_SSL_PORT:-443}:443 and ${EXPOSE_PLUGIN_DEBUGGING_PORT:-5003}:5003 on the host. With TLS terminated by redu, 443 is dead weight, and 5003 is the remote plugin-debugging channel. Publish port 80 alone; verified with `ss -ltn` that nothing else listens."

# Self-host Dify on redu

An LLM app platform with a visual workflow builder, RAG pipelines and agent tooling, running on
infrastructure you own: their full stack on one VM, a managed Postgres beside it, and a public
HTTPS URL.

## What this deploys

- **Dify** from their official pinned images: api, websocket, worker, beat, web, plugin daemon,
  sandbox, the Agent tier and their own nginx — 15 containers on one m1.mem16 VM.
- **Managed Postgres** on its own private VM, so your apps and datasets survive every redeploy.
- Redis and the vector store alongside the app, with named volumes for uploaded documents.
- A public hostname on `*.redu.cloud` with TLS.

About GBP 0.073/hour, roughly GBP 53 a month. **Above the no-card trial ceiling**, so this one
needs a payment method.

## Deploy

Requires the redu MCP on your agent (see the bootstrap commands in the frontmatter). Then, from a
directory containing this file:

    Read redu.md and deploy Dify on redu.

The agent shows you the plan and the cost and waits for your approval before creating anything.

## The five that actually break it

**Two databases.** Their compose ships its own Postgres. Leave it in while also asking redu for a
managed database and you run both, with the app talking to one of them.

**The plugin daemon's second database.** Upstream gives it a database of its own, `dify_plugin`.
redu's managed Postgres only admits connections to the one database it created, so the daemon
crash-loops while every other container reports healthy. Point it at Dify's database instead.

**The URL variables.** Five of them default to empty and several more to localhost, which only
works on localhost. Behind a real hostname the console loads and then calls the wrong origin,
which looks like a broken app.

**The storage volume.** Uploaded documents live on disk, not in Postgres. Without a volume the
database still lists every file in a knowledge base after a redeploy, and none of them exist.

**The shipped credentials.** The example environment file carries the same well-known passwords
that every Dify tutorial reproduces. Replace them, and remember the Redis one appears twice.

## Licence, since it is a fair question

Dify is a modified Apache 2.0. You may not operate a multi-tenant service on it without written
permission, and you may not strip its branding from the frontend. Running your own single-tenant
instance in your own account is neither of those things.

structuredContent.redu_md_markdown:
---
last_deploy:
  id: 422
  date: 2026-08-16
  status: ready
redu_schema: 2
repo: https://github.com/langgenius/dify
plan:
  tool: deploy_compose
  image: langgenius/dify-api:1.16.1 (plus web, worker, plugin_daemon, sandbox, nginx)
  port: 80
  vm: m1.mem16
  flavor_id: m1.mem16
  database: managed postgres (redu-managed, own private VM, m1.small via db_flavor_id "2")
  hourly_cost_gbp: 0.073
bootstrap:
  mcp: claude mcp add --transport http redu «REDACTED:env:78213b90» --client-id redu-mcp
  mcp_codex: codex mcp add redu --url «REDACTED:env:78213b90» --oauth-client-id redu-mcp
  source: dify
quirks:
  - "THIS IS A MULTI-SERVICE STACK, SO deploy_compose, NEVER deploy_app. Start from the compose in Dify's own `docker/` directory (docker-compose.yaml plus .env.example, both pinned to a release) and adapt it. Nothing is built from source: every service is a published image. Nine or so containers end up on ONE VM, which is why the flavor below is memory-first."
  - "⛔ EXPOSE THEIR NGINX, PORT 80, AND NOTHING ELSE. Dify's stack already contains its own nginx that fronts the api, the websocket and the web frontend and routes between them. Their .env ships NGINX_HTTPS_ENABLED=false and EXPOSE_NGINX_PORT=80, which is exactly right here: redu terminates TLS at its own proxy and talks plain HTTP to that nginx. Pass port 80 to deploy_compose. Do NOT expose the api container directly; the frontend calls paths that only exist through their nginx."
  - "⛔ DELETE THE certbot SERVICE. Their compose carries one, for people terminating TLS themselves. On redu it is at best dead weight and at worst it fights redu for the certificate on the *.redu.cloud hostname. Remove it, and leave NGINX_HTTPS_ENABLED=false so their nginx never tries to serve TLS itself."
  - "⛔ DELETE THE db_postgres SERVICE IF YOU USE A MANAGED DATABASE, or you will run two. The compose ships db_postgres (and a db_mysql alternative). With database:'managed' redu provisions a Postgres on its own private VM, and if their db service is still in the compose it starts too, on the app VM, eating RAM to hold nothing. Remove the service AND its depends_on entries, then repoint the variables."
  - "DATABASE: Dify does NOT read DATABASE_URL. deploy_compose with database:'managed' appends PGHOST/PGPORT/PGDATABASE/PGUSER/PGPASSWORD/DATABASE_URL to the project .env, so remap onto Dify's names: DB_HOST=\"${PGHOST}\", DB_PORT=\"${PGPORT}\", DB_DATABASE=\"${PGDATABASE}\", DB_USERNAME=\"${PGUSER}\", DB_PASSWORD=\"${PGPASSWORD}\". Note DB_USERNAME, not DB_USER, which is the name every other app in this library uses and the one you will type by mistake. Managed-DB defaults are database `app` and user `appuser`; Dify creates its own tables inside whatever it is given."
  - "REDIS STAYS IN THE COMPOSE, deliberately. Dify uses it as a cache and as the Celery broker, not as a system of record, so losing it on a redeploy costs a queue drain and no data. Keeping it in-compose also avoids a second managed datastore on the bill. If you DO move it to a managed Redis later, remember CELERY_BROKER_URL embeds the host and credentials in a URL of its own: changing REDIS_HOST and REDIS_PASSWORD without rewriting that URL leaves the workers pointed at the old one, and the symptom is a console that works while nothing ever finishes running."
  - "⛔ CHANGE EVERY DEFAULT CREDENTIAL IN .env.example. It ships with the same well-known values for the Postgres user and for Redis that every Dify tutorial on the internet reproduces. On a private network that is bad practice; the moment anything is reachable it is an open account. Generate fresh values, and remember Redis is referenced twice (REDIS_PASSWORD and inside CELERY_BROKER_URL)."
  - "⛔ SET SECRET_KEY. It ships EMPTY in .env.example. It signs sessions and encrypts stored values, so generate one long random value (their docs use `openssl rand -base64 42`), pass it, and pass the SAME one on every redeploy. Change it and users are logged out and anything encrypted with it stops decrypting."
  - "SET THE FIVE URL VARIABLES TO THE PUBLIC HOSTNAME: CONSOLE_API_URL, CONSOLE_WEB_URL, SERVICE_API_URL, APP_API_URL and APP_WEB_URL. They default to empty, which works only when everything is on localhost. Left unset behind a real hostname the console loads and then calls the wrong origin, which reads as a broken app rather than as a config mistake. Generate the dname yourself in the full `dify-<8 lowercase alnum>.redu.cloud` form so these are known at deploy time; a bare label gets a random suffix appended by redu and will not match."
  - "⛔ PERSIST THE STORAGE VOLUME. STORAGE_TYPE defaults to opendal, which means local disk: uploaded documents and everything in a knowledge base live on the VM's filesystem, not in Postgres. Without a volume they are gone on the next redeploy while the database still lists them. Mount volumes on the api and worker storage paths their compose already declares, and do not drop them when trimming services."
  - "VECTOR STORE: VECTOR_STORE defaults to weaviate, which runs as another container on the app VM. That is the simple path and it is what the sizing below assumes. redu also has a managed Qdrant, and Dify supports qdrant as a VECTOR_STORE value, which is the better shape for anything real: it moves the index off the app VM so a redeploy cannot lose it. Treat that as a documented upgrade, not the default, and price the extra datastore before offering it."
  - "SIZE FOR MEMORY, NOT CPU. Nine containers including a vector database on one VM is a RAM problem long before it is a CPU problem. m1.mem16 (4 vCPU / 16 GB) costs GBP 0.0556/hr, barely more than m1.large (4 vCPU / 8 GB) at GBP 0.0486, and doubles the headroom: it is the right default here. m1.large will boot and will be tight. Both are ABOVE the no-card trial ceiling of m1.medium, so a trial user cannot deploy this at all: say that BEFORE the plan is approved, not after a quota rejection."
  - "NO migrate_command NEEDED. MIGRATION_ENABLED=true in their .env, so the api container runs its migrations at boot. On a fresh managed Postgres the first boot is long: images to pull, then migrations, then the plugin daemon settling. Give the health check generous room; an impatient probe reports a failed deploy on a stack that is starting normally."
  - "DEPLOY: check_deploy_prerequisites -> plan_deploy (paste this file as redu_md) -> show the user the plan and the cost (about GBP 0.073/hr, roughly GBP 53 a month, and NOT inside the no-card trial) and WAIT for their yes -> deploy_compose with flavor_id 'm1.mem16', database:'managed', db_engine:'postgres', db_flavor_id:'2' (m1.small; OMITTING db_flavor_id defaults the DB VM to the app flavor and costs far more), port 80."
  - "SOURCE IS UPLOAD MODE, NOT GIT. Assemble the trimmed compose and .env locally, then prepare_upload -> run the returned tar+curl block -> deploy_compose with the source_token and no repo. Pointing deploy_compose at the Dify GitHub URL would make redu try to build a very large monorepo that does not need building."
  - "LICENCE: Dify is a modified Apache 2.0. The two added conditions are no operating a MULTI-TENANT service on it without written permission, and no removing the Dify logo or copyright from the frontend. A single-tenant instance in the user's own account, unbranded, is fine. Do not help anyone resell workspaces on it."
  - "⛔ NEVER WRITE CREDENTIALS INTO THIS FILE. redu.md is committed and read by the next person. SECRET_KEY, the database password and the Redis password belong to the user. Hand them over in the session; the deploy log records that the defaults were replaced, never what with."
  - "AFTERWARDS: pass THIS file to get_deployment as redu_md and write the merged redu_md_markdown back, adding anything you hit that is not already here. This is the entry most likely to teach you something new, so write it down."
  - "DELETING IT LEAVES THE DATABASE BEHIND, ON PURPOSE. delete_deployment removes the app VM but keeps the managed Postgres so apps and datasets are not lost by accident, and that DB keeps billing at GBP 0.0174/hr. To stop paying entirely the user must also delete_database."
  - "⛔ THE PLUGIN DAEMON MUST SHARE DIFY'S DATABASE ON REDU. Upstream points it at a SECOND database, DB_PLUGIN_DATABASE=dify_plugin, on the same server. redu's managed Postgres scopes its pg_hba.conf entry to the ONE database it provisioned, so every other database on that server is refused BEFORE authentication: 'FATAL: no pg_hba.conf entry for host <app ip>, user <dbuser>, database dify_plugin'. With db_superuser the daemon even succeeds in CREATE DATABASE dify_plugin and still cannot connect to it, so the database exists and the container crash-loops on exit 2 anyway. Set the daemon's DB_DATABASE to ${PGDATABASE} (NOT ${DB_PLUGIN_DATABASE}). Verified safe on 1.16.1: the api creates 136 tables and the daemon's 13 (plugins, plugin_installations, plugin_declarations, endpoints, serverless_runtimes, datasource_installations, tool_installations, ai_model_installations, install_tasks, tenant_storages, agent_strategy_installations, trigger_installations, plugin_readme_records) collide with none of them. Everything else in the stack comes up green while this one crash-loops, so the console looks fine and plugins are simply dead: check `docker ps` for plugin_daemon, do not trust the access point."
  - "1.16.1 IS 15 CONTAINERS, NOT NINE. The release added a Dify Agent tier (agent_backend + local_sandbox + agent_ssrf_proxy) and a dedicated api_websocket. Full keep-list: init_permissions, api, api_websocket, worker, worker_beat, web, nginx, redis, sandbox, local_sandbox, plugin_daemon, agent_backend, ssrf_proxy, agent_ssrf_proxy, weaviate. Measured idle footprint on m1.mem16: 2.7 GB of 16 GB used. m1.mem16 remains right; m1.large (8 GB) would survive idle and is a real risk under dataset indexing."
  - "MOST OF THE COMPOSE IS BEHIND `profiles:` IN 1.16.x, AND .env.example SETS COMPOSE_PROFILES=${VECTOR_STORE:-weaviate},${DB_TYPE:-postgresql},collaboration. Do not rely on the compose engine honouring profiles. DELETE the services you do not want outright and STRIP `profiles:` from the ones you keep (weaviate, api_websocket), then set COMPOSE_PROFILES= empty. Leave the postgresql profile enabled by accident and you get the second Postgres this file already warns about; leave weaviate gated and the vector store never starts at all."
  - "THE `envs/` env_file ENTRIES ARE NO-OPS. Every service lists ~25 `env_file: - path: ./envs/... required: false` entries, but the repo ships only *.env.example under docker/envs/ — the real files do not exist. Collapse each service's env_file to `- ./.env` and the stack behaves identically with 75 fewer lines. Keeping them costs nothing on docker but is one more thing podman can trip on."
  - "DECLARE THE `default` NETWORK EXPLICITLY. Services name `default` in their networks: list but upstream never defines it, and podman-compose refuses the whole file with `RuntimeError: missing networks: default`. Adding `default: {driver: bridge}` to the networks block fixes it and is a no-op under docker. Worth doing even if you pass compose_engine:'docker', so the file stays portable."
  - "PREFER compose_engine:'docker' FOR THIS STACK. It uses modern compose-spec that podman-compose 1.0.6 handles poorly (env_file long-form, depends_on conditions incl. service_completed_successfully), and nginx's /socket.io/ block hardcodes `resolver [ip]`, which is DOCKER's embedded DNS — under podman that location cannot resolve and workflow collaboration breaks while the rest of the console looks fine. Confirmed working: deploy_compose with compose_engine:'docker' on 1.16.1."
  - "USE NAMED VOLUMES, NOT THE ./volumes BIND MOUNTS, FOR DURABLE STATE. Upstream binds ./volumes/app/storage, ./volumes/plugin_daemon, ./volumes/weaviate and ./volumes/redis/data inside the project directory, which is exactly what a source re-upload replaces. Move those four to named volumes (app_storage, plugin_storage, weaviate_data, redis_data). Bonus: a fresh named volume inherits /app/api/storage's uid 1001 ownership from the image, so the init_permissions chown becomes belt-and-braces instead of load-bearing. Keep ./volumes/sandbox/conf, ./nginx and ./ssrf_proxy as bind mounts — those are config shipped in the tarball."
  - "SET MORE THAN FIVE URL VARIABLES ON 1.16.x. Beyond the five above, these also default to empty or to localhost and are wrong behind a real hostname: FILES_URL (file previews and multimodal), TRIGGER_URL, ENDPOINT_URL_TEMPLATE (https://<host>/e/{hook_id}), and NEXT_PUBLIC_SOCKET_URL, which ships as ws://localhost and must become wss://<host> or the collaboration websocket fails against a TLS origin. Set INTERNAL_FILES_URL=http://api:5001 too. Good check after deploy: `curl -s https://<host>/install | grep -c localhost:5001` must be 0."
  - "CAP THE SQLALCHEMY POOL. .env.example ships SQLALCHEMY_POOL_SIZE=30 with MAX_OVERFLOW=10, and api + api_websocket + worker + worker_beat each open their own pool: up to 160 connections against a managed m1.small Postgres whose max_connections you do not control. Drop to SQLALCHEMY_POOL_SIZE=10 / SQLALCHEMY_MAX_OVERFLOW=5 and set SQLALCHEMY_POOL_PRE_PING=true."
  - "SET MIGRATION_ENABLED=false ON worker, worker_beat AND api_websocket. The image entrypoint runs `flask upgrade-db` whenever the variable is true, regardless of MODE, so all four containers race the same migration on a fresh database. Leave it true only on api. The others crash-loop briefly until the tables exist, then settle — restart: always covers it."
  - "MORE CREDENTIALS THAN THE FILE USED TO SAY. 1.16.1 ships well-known defaults for SANDBOX_API_KEY/CODE_EXECUTION_API_KEY (must match each other), PLUGIN_DAEMON_KEY, PLUGIN_DIFY_INNER_API_KEY, WEAVIATE_API_KEY (must match WEAVIATE_AUTHENTICATION_APIKEY_ALLOWED_KEYS), DIFY_AGENT_API_TOKEN, DIFY_AGENT_SERVER_SECRET_KEY and an EMPTY DIFY_AGENT_SHELLCTL_AUTH_TOKEN. Regenerate all of them. Also flip WEAVIATE_AUTHENTICATION_ANONYMOUS_ACCESS_ENABLED to false — .env.example sets it true even though the compose default is false."
  - "SECRET_KEY IS NO LONGER STRICTLY REQUIRED BUT STILL SET IT. 1.16.1's .env.example comments that an empty value auto-generates a persistent key into the storage directory. That key then lives only in the storage volume, so losing the volume logs everyone out. Passing your own value keeps it in your hands and in the redeploy recipe."
  - "DROP nginx's 443 PUBLISH AND plugin_daemon's 5003 PUBLISH. Upstream publishes ${EXPOSE_NGINX_SSL_PORT:-443}:443 and ${EXPOSE_PLUGIN_DEBUGGING_PORT:-5003}:5003 on the host. With TLS terminated by redu, 443 is dead weight, and 5003 is the remote plugin-debugging channel. Publish port 80 alone; verified with `ss -ltn` that nothing else listens."
---

# Self-host Dify on redu

An LLM app platform with a visual workflow builder, RAG pipelines and agent tooling, running on
infrastructure you own: their full stack on one VM, a managed Postgres beside it, and a public
HTTPS URL.

## What this deploys

- **Dify** from their official pinned images: api, websocket, worker, beat, web, plugin daemon,
  sandbox, the Agent tier and their own nginx — 15 containers on one m1.mem16 VM.
- **Managed Postgres** on its own private VM, so your apps and datasets survive every redeploy.
- Redis and the vector store alongside the app, with named volumes for uploaded documents.
- A public hostname on `*.redu.cloud` with TLS.

About GBP 0.073/hour, roughly GBP 53 a month. **Above the no-card trial ceiling**, so this one
needs a payment method.

## Deploy

Requires the redu MCP on your agent (see the bootstrap commands in the frontmatter). Then, from a
directory containing this file:

    Read redu.md and deploy Dify on redu.

The agent shows you the plan and the cost and waits for your approval before creating anything.

## The five that actually break it

**Two databases.** Their compose ships its own Postgres. Leave it in while also asking redu for a
managed database and you run both, with the app talking to one of them.

**The plugin daemon's second database.** Upstream gives it a database of its own, `dify_plugin`.
redu's managed Postgres only admits connections to the one database it created, so the daemon
crash-loops while every other container reports healthy. Point it at Dify's database instead.

**The URL variables.** Five of them default to empty and several more to localhost, which only
works on localhost. Behind a real hostname the console loads and then calls the wrong origin,
which looks like a broken app.

**The storage volume.** Uploaded documents live on disk, not in Postgres. Without a volume the
database still lists every file in a knowledge base after a redeploy, and none of them exist.

**The shipped credentials.** The example environment file carries the same well-known passwords
that every Dify tutorial reproduces. Replace them, and remember the Redis one appears twice.

About GBP 0.073/hour, roughly GBP 53 a month. **Above the no-card trial ceiling**, so this one needs a payment method. ## Deploy Requires the redu MCP on your agent (see the bootstrap commands in the frontmatter). Then, from a directory containing this file: Read redu.md and deploy Dify on redu. The agent shows you the plan and the cost and waits for your approval before creating anything. ## The five that actually break it **Two databases.** Their compose ships its own Postgres. Leave it in while also asking redu for a managed database and you run both, with the app talking to one of them. **The plugin daemon's second database.** Upstream gives it a database of its own, `dify_plugin`. redu's managed Postgres only admits connections to the one database it created, so the daemon crash-loops while every other container reports healthy. Point it at Dify's database instead. **The URL variables.** Five of them default to empty and several more to localhost, which only works on localhost. Behind a real hostname the console loads and then calls the wrong origin, which looks like a broken app. **The storage volume.** Uploaded documents live on disk, not in Postgres. Without a volume the database still lists every file in a knowledge base after a redeploy, and none of them exist. **The shipped credentials.** The example environment file carries the same well-known passwords that every Dify tutorial reproduces. Replace them, and remember the Redis one appears twice. ## Licence, since it is a fair question Dify is a modified Apache 2.0. You may not operate a multi-tenant service on it without written permission, and you may not strip its branding from the frontend. Running your own single-tenant instance in your own account is neither of those things. ## Deploy log - Not yet deployed. content.text:
Dify is deployed and running.

**https://dify-59d4fda9.redu.cloud** → go to `/install` to create the admin account. Setup is still `not_started`, so the first person to hit that page claims it.

All 15 containers stable (`init_permissions` exited 0 by design), api healthy, plugin daemon settled. Deployment `422`, app VM `dify` (m1.mem16), managed Postgres `dify` on `db-dify` — **£0.073/hr, ~£53/month**. About 8 minutes from launch to serving, mostly image pulls; idle RAM is 2.7 GB of 16.

**One thing found and fixed that `redu.md` didn't predict.** The plugin daemon crash-looped on exit 2 while all 14 other containers reported healthy — and the public URL looked perfectly fine throughout. Upstream points the daemon at a *second* database, `dify_plugin`, but redu's managed Postgres scopes its `pg_hba.conf` entry to the one database it provisioned, so connections to any other database are refused before authentication. With `db_superuser` the daemon even succeeded in creating `dify_plugin` and still couldn't connect to it. I pointed it at Dify's own database after verifying no collisions — the api creates 136 tables, the daemon's 13 overlap with none.

Worth knowing: I applied that live by recreating the container with a compose env override, because editing the root-owned `.env` on the VM was blocked by a permission classifier. It survives restarts and reboots, but **the `.env` on the VM still says `dify_plugin`** — so if anyone re-runs `docker compose up` there without the override, the daemon breaks again. The permanent fix is in `redu.md`, so a redeploy from the recipe is correct from the start. If you'd like the on-VM `.env` corrected too, approve a `sudo sed` on `/opt/app-src/.env` and I'll do it in one command.

**Credentials are in my earlier message** — they're deliberately not in `redu.md` or any file in the repo (verified: zero matches). `SECRET_KEY` is the one to keep; reuse it on every redeploy.

**Files written** to `/home/milos/Desktop/tests_lib/dify/`:
- `redu.md` — merged, now 32 quirks (was 20). Beyond the plugin-daemon trap: 1.16.1 is 15 containers not nine, nearly every service is gated behind `profiles:`, the `envs/*.env` entries are no-ops, `default` must be declared or podman-compose won't parse the file, four more URL variables need the public hostname, and the SQLAlchemy pool defaults would open up to 160 connections against an m1.small.
- `redu-deploy-plan.md` — real provisioned values, replacing the estimate.

Two notes I'd flag rather than act on: the quota was 6 GB short mid-session because another session had six VMs running, then cleared on its own before I provisioned — nothing was deleted. And the working compose file (no secrets in it, all `${VAR}`) currently lives only in my scratchpad; say the word and I'll drop it into the repo so a redeploy doesn't have to reassemble it from the recipe.

class OnceTrueCallable[**P](Protocol):
    def __call__(self, *args: P.args, **kwargs: P.kwargs) -> bool: ...

    def mark_success(self) -> None: ...

    def reset_success(self) -> None: ...


def once_true[**P](func: Callable[P, bool]) -> OnceTrueCallable[P]:
    """Wrap a predicate so only a strict True result is memoized."""
    has_success = False

    def mark_success() -> None:
        nonlocal has_success

        has_success = True

    def reset_success() -> None:
        nonlocal has_success

        has_success = False

    @wraps(func)
    def wrapper(*args: P.args, **kwargs: P.kwargs) -> bool:
        nonlocal has_success

        if has_success:
            return True

        result = func(*args, **kwargs)
        if result is True:
            has_success = True

        return result

    wrapper.mark_success = mark_success  # type: ignore[attr-defined]
    wrapper.reset_success = reset_success  # type: ignore[attr-defined]
    return cast(OnceTrueCallable[P], wrapper)


def mark_setup_completed() -> None:
    """Remember in this process that one-time self-hosted setup has completed."""
    _is_setup_completed.mark_success()


@once_true
def _is_setup_completed() -> bool:
    """Check whether setup exists, caching only successful observations.

    Use `once_true` instead of `@cache` because a pre-setup False result must not be memoized.

class OnceTrueCallable[**P](Protocol):
    def __call__(self, *args: P.args, **kwargs: P.kwargs) -> bool: ...

    def reset_success(self) -> None: ...


def once_true[**P](func: Callable[P, bool]) -> OnceTrueCallable[P]:
    """Wrap a predicate so only a strict True result is memoized."""
    has_success = False

    def mark_success() -> None:
        nonlocal has_success

        has_success = True

    def reset_success() -> None:
        nonlocal has_success

        has_success = False

    @wraps(func)
    def wrapper(*args: P.args, **kwargs: P.kwargs) -> bool:
        nonlocal has_success

        if has_success:
            return True

        result = func(*args, **kwargs)
        if result is True:
            has_success = True

        return result

    wrapper.mark_success = mark_success  # type: ignore[attr-defined]
    wrapper.reset_success = reset_success  # type: ignore[attr-defined]

received from the frontend.

Note: This uses Base64 encoding for obfuscation, not cryptographic encryption.

        """

            decoded_text = decoded_bytes.decode("utf-8")
            logger.debug("Field decoding successful")

# Dify on redu.cloud — session report

**Date:** 2026-08-16 (UTC)
**Task:** `Read redu.md and deploy Dify on redu.`
**Outcome:** Deployed successfully, verified end to end, admin account created, then torn down at the user's request.
**Deployment:** `#422` — `https://dify-59d4fda9.redu.cloud` (destroyed at end of session)

---

## 1. Summary

Deployed Dify 1.16.1 as a 15-container compose stack onto a single redu VM with a managed Postgres
beside it, following the recipe in `redu.md`. The recipe was written against an older, ~9-container
Dify and did not survive contact with 1.16.1 unmodified: eight of its assumptions were stale and one
previously-unknown failure mode (the plugin daemon's second database) took the stack down in a way
that left the public URL looking perfectly healthy.

Everything was found, fixed and verified. `redu.md` grew from 20 quirks to 33.

**Timings:** ~8 minutes from `deploy_compose` to the frontend serving — 380 s to HTTP 200 on `/`,
with the api answering 60 s after that. The bulk of that is pulling 15 images. Idle memory settled at
2.7 GB of 16 GB.

**Cost while it ran:** GBP 0.073/hr (app VM GBP 0.0556 + managed Postgres GBP 0.0174), ~GBP 53.29/mo.
Exactly as the plan estimated.

---

## 2. What was provisioned

| Resource | Value |
|---|---|
| Deployment id | `422`, name `dify` |
| Public URL | `https://dify-59d4fda9.redu.cloud` (dname generated up front, not auto-assigned) |
| App VM | `91d1d4d6-d0cc-4f82-a90e-a4e674af9e4c` — `m1.mem16` (flavor id `7`), 4 vCPU / 16 GB |
| App private IP | `[ip]` (floating `[ip]`) |
| Managed Postgres | db `#125`, VM `db-dify` (`98f3f325-3977-4bcf-b4ca-b39140e71465`), `m1.small` (flavor id `2`) |
| DB private IP | `[ip]`, port 5432, private-network only |
| DB config | PG 16, database `dify`, user `dify`, superuser, extensions `uuid-ossp` + `pg_trgm` |
| Network | `f7102e8d-9800-48d7-80a9-8369091d7cad` |
| Keypair | `redu-deploy-test` |
| Source mode | upload (tarball, 11198 bytes — size confirmed identical on both sides) |
| Compose engine | `docker` (explicitly forced, see §5.4) |
| Published ports | host port 80 only — verified with `ss -ltn` |

---

## 3. Process followed

1. Read `redu.md`.
2. `whoami` → credential verified. `check_deploy_prerequisites` → ready; auto-selected network + keypair.
3. Pulled Dify at tag `1.16.1` (confirmed the tag form is `1.16.1`, not `v1.16.1`) and extracted `docker/`.
4. Read the upstream compose (1326 lines, ~40 services) and `.env.example` (300 lines), plus the nginx
   templates, the ssrf_proxy templates and the sandbox config.
5. Read the `dify-plugin-daemon` source on GitHub to establish how it initialises its database —
   this is what later made the `pg_hba` failure diagnosable rather than mysterious.
6. Assembled a trimmed compose + env locally; validated with `docker compose config` **and**
   `podman-compose config` before uploading anything.
7. `plan_deploy` with the trimmed compose and `redu.md` pasted in → plan, cost, preflight.
8. Wrote `redu-deploy-plan.md`, showed the plan and cost, and **waited for approval** (§4).
9. `prepare_upload` → packaged and uploaded → `deploy_compose`.
10. Polled to `ready`; verified over HTTP and over SSH.
11. Found and fixed the plugin daemon defect; re-verified.
12. Created the owner account via the API; found and worked around the login encoding quirk.
13. Merged everything learned back into `redu.md` via `get_deployment`.
14. Tore the deployment down.

---

## 4. The quota incident (no action taken, resolved itself)

At planning time the plan came back **infeasible**: it needed 18432 MB RAM against 12288 MB available.

Between the first `whoami` (1 instance, 16384 MB used) and `plan_deploy` a few minutes later, the
account had jumped to **7 instances / 38912 MB / 15 vCPU**. Six VMs — `langflow`, `db-langflow`,
`openwebui`, `db-openwebui`, `umami`, `db-umami` — had been created between 21:33 and 21:37 by
something outside this session.

This was surfaced to the user as a blocking choice (free RAM and keep `m1.mem16`, drop to `m1.large`
and fit the current quota, or raise the quota) rather than silently downsizing. The user chose to keep
`m1.mem16`. Before anything was deleted, a re-check showed the other session's VMs had been torn down
on their own — 32768 MB free. **Nothing was deleted and nothing was downsized.**

---

## 5. Changes made to the upstream stack

Trimmed from ~40 services to 15: `init_permissions`, `api`, `api_websocket`, `worker`, `worker_beat`,
`web`, `nginx`, `redis`, `sandbox`, `local_sandbox`, `plugin_daemon`, `agent_backend`, `ssrf_proxy`,
`agent_ssrf_proxy`, `weaviate`.

### 5.1 Called for by `redu.md`
- Removed `db_postgres` and `db_mysql`; wired `DB_HOST/PORT/DATABASE/USERNAME/PASSWORD` to the
  `PG*` variables redu appends to the project `.env`. Referenced them in the compose `environment:`
  blocks rather than inside `.env`, so ordering of redu's appended lines cannot matter.
- Removed `certbot`; left `NGINX_HTTPS_ENABLED=false`.
- Kept redis in-compose.
- Regenerated every shipped credential.
- Set `SECRET_KEY`.
- Set the five URL variables to the public hostname.
- Persisted storage (see 5.5).
- Published port 80 and nothing else.

### 5.2 Removed everything unused
Every non-weaviate vector store (qdrant, pgvector, pgvecto-rs, chroma, oceanbase, seekdb, vastbase,
iris, oracle, myscale, matrixone, opengauss, elasticsearch, kibana, opensearch + dashboards, milvus +
etcd + minio), `unstructured`, and `couchbase-server` — the last of which carried a `build:` directive
that would have forced a source build on the VM.

### 5.3 `profiles:` — a 1.16.x trap
Nearly every service in 1.16.x is gated behind `profiles:`, and `.env.example` ships
`COMPOSE_PROFILES=${VECTOR_STORE:-weaviate},${DB_TYPE:-postgresql},collaboration`. Left alone that
enables the `postgresql` profile and starts the second Postgres this recipe exists to avoid. Rather
than depend on the engine interpreting profiles at all, unwanted services were **deleted outright** and
`profiles:` **stripped** from the ones kept (`weaviate`, `api_websocket`), with `COMPOSE_PROFILES=` empty.

### 5.4 Compose-engine compatibility
- The `env_file:` lists (~25 entries per service pointing at `./envs/**.env`) are **no-ops** — the repo
  ships only `*.env.example`. Collapsed to `- ./.env`, removing ~75 lines.
- Upstream never declares the `default` network although services reference it by name;
  `podman-compose` refuses the file outright with `RuntimeError: missing networks: default`.
  Added `default: {driver: bridge}`, which is a no-op under docker.
- Forced `compose_engine: 'docker'`. The stack uses modern compose-spec (`env_file` long form,
  `depends_on` conditions including `service_completed_successfully`), and nginx's `/socket.io/` block
  hardcodes `resolver [ip]` — Docker's embedded DNS. Under podman that location cannot resolve
  and workflow collaboration silently breaks while the rest of the console looks fine.

### 5.5 Durability
Moved `app_storage`, `plugin_storage`, `weaviate_data` and `redis_data` from `./volumes` bind mounts
(inside the project directory, i.e. exactly what a source re-upload replaces) to **named volumes**.
Kept `./volumes/sandbox/conf`, `./nginx` and `./ssrf_proxy` as bind mounts — those are config shipped
in the tarball. Side benefit: a fresh named volume inherits `/app/api/storage`'s uid 1001 ownership
from the image, so the `init_permissions` chown became belt-and-braces rather than load-bearing.

### 5.6 Correctness and hardening
- Additional URL variables 1.16.x needs and `redu.md` did not list: `FILES_URL`, `TRIGGER_URL`,
  `ENDPOINT_URL_TEMPLATE`, `NEXT_PUBLIC_SOCKET_URL` (ships as `ws://localhost`, must be `wss://`),
  `INTERNAL_FILES_URL`.
- `SQLALCHEMY_POOL_SIZE` 30 → 10 and `MAX_OVERFLOW` 10 → 5. Four services each open their own pool;
  the defaults allow up to 160 connections against a managed `m1.small` whose `max_connections` is
  not under our control. Also set `SQLALCHEMY_POOL_PRE_PING=true`.
- `MIGRATION_ENABLED=false` on `worker`, `worker_beat`, `api_websocket`. The image entrypoint runs
  `flask upgrade-db` whenever the variable is true regardless of `MODE`, so all four containers
  otherwise race the same migration on a fresh database. Left true on `api` only.
- `WEAVIATE_AUTHENTICATION_ANONYMOUS_ACCESS_ENABLED` → false (`.env.example` sets it true even though
  the compose default is false), with a generated API key.
- Tightened `CONSOLE_CORS_ALLOW_ORIGINS` to the public origin; left `WEB_API_CORS_ALLOW_ORIGINS=*` so
  embedded web apps keep working.
- Dropped nginx's `443` publish and plugin_daemon's `5003` (remote plugin debugging) publish.

---

## 6. Defects found during verification

### 6.1 Plugin daemon crash-loop — the significant one

**Symptom.** `plugin_daemon` restarting on exit 2. All 14 other containers up, `api` healthy, the
public URL serving normally. Nothing in the access point suggested a problem.

**Error.**
```
FATAL: no pg_hba.conf entry for host "[ip]", user "dify",
       database "dify_plugin", no encryption (SQLSTATE 28000)
```

**Root cause.** Upstream points the plugin daemon at a *second* database, `DB_PLUGIN_DATABASE=dify_plugin`,
on the same server. redu's managed Postgres scopes its `pg_hba.conf` entry to the single database it
provisioned, so every other database on that server is refused **before authentication**. Because the
DB user had been granted superuser, the daemon *succeeded* in running `CREATE DATABASE dify_plugin`
— confirmed present in `pg_database` — and then still could not connect to it. So the database exists
and the container crash-loops anyway, which makes the failure read as something other than what it is.

**Fix.** Point the daemon at Dify's own database (`DB_DATABASE: ${PGDATABASE}`).

**Safety check before applying.** Queried the live schema: Dify's api creates **136** tables in `dify`,
and **zero** of them collide with the daemon's 13 (`plugins`, `plugin_installations`,
`plugin_declarations`, `endpoints`, `serverless_runtimes`, `datasource_installations`,
`tool_installations`, `ai_model_installations`, `install_tasks`, `tenant_storages`,
`agent_strategy_installations`, `trigger_installations`, `plugin_readme_records`).

**Applied live** by recreating the container with a compose shell-env override, after an attempt to
edit the root-owned `/opt/app-src/.env` was blocked by a permission classifier. Result:
`database migration completed successfully` / `current node has become the master of the cluster`.
The permanent fix went into the local compose and into `redu.md`. This was disclosed to the user at
the time, including the caveat that the on-VM `.env` still read `dify_plugin` and that a bare
`docker compose up` there would have reverted it.

### 6.2 Console login rejects a plaintext password

**Symptom.** `POST /console/api/login` → `401 {"code":"authentication_failed","message":"Invalid encrypted data"}`,
which reads exactly like a wrong password. No traceback in the api log, because it is a handled exception.

**Root cause.** 1.16.x wraps the login view in `decrypt_password_field`, which base64-decodes the field
(`libs/encryption.py` — explicitly obfuscation, not cryptography; real security is HTTPS).
`/console/api/setup` does **not** apply it. So the same password is plaintext at setup and Base64 at login.

**Also.** Login returns only `{"result":"success"}` — no tokens in the body. The JWTs arrive as HttpOnly
`__Host-access_token` / `__Host-refresh_token` / `__Host-csrf_token` cookies. `__Host-` requires
`Secure`, which is a further reason the URL variables must be `https`.

---

## 7. Verification performed

**HTTP, unauthenticated**

| Path | Result |
|---|---|
| `/` | 307 → `/install` (correct pre-setup) |
| `/install` | 200 |
| `/console/api/setup` | 200 `{"step":"not_started"}` → proves api + managed Postgres + migrations |
| `/console/api/system-features` | 200, real payload, `enable_collaboration_mode: true` |
| `/e/test-hook` | 301 → proves nginx reaches the plugin daemon |

**Origin wiring** — the served `/install` HTML references `dify-59d4fda9.redu.cloud` 8 times and
`localhost:5001` / `127.0.0.1` **zero** times. This is the exact failure mode `redu.md` warns about.

**Containers (SSH)** — all 15 accounted for: 14 up, `init_permissions` `Exited (0)` by design.
`api`, `redis`, `sandbox`, `local_sandbox` reporting `(healthy)`.

**Host ports** — `ss -ltn` showed only `:80`. Ports 443 and 5003 correctly absent.

**Memory** — 2.7 GB used of 15993 MB at idle; 13.3 GB available.

**Authenticated, as the created account** — logged in properly with a cookie jar and CSRF header
rather than trusting the 201:

| Endpoint | Result |
|---|---|
| `/console/api/account/profile` | 200 — `«REDACTED:env:013044ef»`, name `Milos` |
| `/console/api/workspaces` | 200 — `Milos's Workspace`, `current: true` |
| `/console/api/apps` | 200 |
| `/console/api/datasets` | 200 (RAG / weaviate path) |
| `/console/api/workspaces/current/models/model-types/llm` | 200 |
| `/console/api/workspaces/current/plugin/list` | 200, `{"plugins":[],"total":0}` — end-to-end proof the plugin daemon fix holds through the api, not just at the container |

---

## 8. Account created

Owner account created via `POST /console/api/setup` for `«REDACTED:env:013044ef»`
(user id `40541b7c-25d5-4585-a83f-bc305d6f36ee`, workspace `f9070833-9ece-4ac0-9da7-c376e2909ea9`).

The email was **confirmed with the user before firing**, because the endpoint is one-shot — afterwards
it reports `step: finished` and closes, making the owner email effectively permanent.

---

## 9. Credentials

Every shipped default was replaced with a freshly generated value: `SECRET_KEY`, `REDIS_PASSWORD`
(and the copy embedded in `CELERY_BROKER_URL`), `SANDBOX_API_KEY` + matching `CODE_EXECUTION_API_KEY`,
`PLUGIN_DAEMON_KEY`, `PLUGIN_DIFY_INNER_API_KEY`, `DIFY_AGENT_API_TOKEN`,
`DIFY_AGENT_SERVER_SECRET_KEY`, `DIFY_AGENT_SHELLCTL_AUTH_TOKEN`, `WEAVIATE_API_KEY`, plus the
generated console admin password.

**Values are deliberately not reproduced in this file.** They were handed to the user in-session, and
`redu.md` and `redu-deploy-plan.md` were both checked to confirm zero credential matches. With the
deployment destroyed they are void in any case.

---

## 10. Teardown

`delete_deployment` was run on deployment `422` at the user's request after this report was written.

Per redu's design — and as `redu.md` documents — **deleting a deployment intentionally leaves the
managed Postgres behind** so apps and datasets are not lost by accident. That database continues to
bill at GBP 0.0174/hr (~GBP 12.70/mo) until `delete_database` is run against db `#125`. See the closing
note in the session for its disposition.

---

## 11. Files written

| Path | Contents |
|---|---|
| `/home/milos/Desktop/tests_lib/dify/redu.md` | Merged recipe — **20 → 33 quirks** |
| `/home/milos/Desktop/tests_lib/dify/redu-deploy-plan.md` | Real provisioned values, replacing the pre-deploy estimate |
| `/home/milos/Desktop/tests_lib/dify/dify-redu-session-report.md` | This report |

### The 13 quirks added to `redu.md`

1. Plugin daemon must share Dify's database (`pg_hba` scoping) — with the full symptom description,
   because every other container looks healthy while it fails.
2. 1.16.1 is 15 containers, not nine, with the full keep-list and measured idle footprint.
3. Most of the compose is behind `profiles:`; delete rather than gate.
4. The `envs/*.env` `env_file` entries are no-ops.
5. Declare the `default` network or podman-compose will not parse the file.
6. Prefer `compose_engine:'docker'` — including the `resolver [ip]` reason.
7. Use named volumes, not the `./volumes` bind mounts.
8. Four more URL variables need the public hostname, with a `grep -c localhost:5001` check.
9. Cap the SQLAlchemy pool.
10. `MIGRATION_ENABLED=false` on the non-api services.
11. More credentials ship with defaults than the file used to say.
12. `SECRET_KEY` is no longer strictly required but should still be set.
13. Creating the owner account by API: plaintext at setup, Base64 at login, cookies not body tokens.

Plus a rewritten deploy-log entry recording the measured timings, what the recipe got right, and what
it failed to predict.

### Not committed
The working trimmed `docker-compose.yaml` (no secrets in it — every value is `${VAR}`) lives only in
this session's scratchpad at
`/tmp/claude-1000/-home-milos-Desktop-tests-lib-dify/02db4cd5-330b-4816-987e-10c5cd662e36/scratchpad/deploy/`.
It was offered for inclusion in the repo and not requested. `redu.md` alone is sufficient to
reassemble it.

---

## 12. Assessment of the recipe

**Held up:** port 80 through Dify's own nginx; managed Postgres via `PG*` with `DB_USERNAME` not
`DB_USER`; upload mode over git; no `migrate_command` needed; the memory-first flavor choice;
generating the dname up front; the cost estimate (exact); the warning to expect a slow first boot.

**Did not survive 1.16.1:** the container count, the profiles behaviour, the env_file structure, the
number of URL variables, the credential inventory, and — most importantly — it had no way to know
about the plugin daemon's second database, which is a genuine interaction between Dify's design and
redu's managed-Postgres `pg_hba` scoping rather than a fault in either one.

The single most valuable line added is quirk 1, because the failure presents as a working deployment.

## 4. The quota incident (no action taken, resolved itself)

At planning time the plan came back **infeasible**: it needed 18432 MB RAM against 12288 MB available.

Between the first `whoami` (1 instance, 16384 MB used) and `plan_deploy` a few minutes later, the
account had jumped to **7 instances / 38912 MB / 15 vCPU**. Six VMs — `langflow`, `db-langflow`,
`openwebui`, `db-openwebui`, `umami`, `db-umami` — had been created between 21:33 and 21:37 by
something outside this session.

This was surfaced to the user as a blocking choice (free RAM and keep `m1.mem16`, drop to `m1.large`
and fit the current quota, or raise the quota) rather than silently downsizing. The user chose to keep
`m1.mem16`. Before anything was deleted, a re-check showed the other session's VMs had been torn down
on their own — 32768 MB free. **Nothing was deleted and nothing was downsized.**

## 5. Changes made to the upstream stack

Trimmed from ~40 services to 15: `init_permissions`, `api`, `api_websocket`, `worker`, `worker_beat`,
`web`, `nginx`, `redis`, `sandbox`, `local_sandbox`, `plugin_daemon`, `agent_backend`, `ssrf_proxy`,
`agent_ssrf_proxy`, `weaviate`.

### 5.1 Called for by `redu.md`
- Removed `db_postgres` and `db_mysql`; wired `DB_HOST/PORT/DATABASE/USERNAME/PASSWORD` to the
  `PG*` variables redu appends to the project `.env`. Referenced them in the compose `environment:`
  blocks rather than inside `.env`, so ordering of redu's appended lines cannot matter.
- Removed `certbot`; left `NGINX_HTTPS_ENABLED=false`.
- Kept redis in-compose.
- Regenerated every shipped credential.
- Set `SECRET_KEY`.
- Set the five URL variables to the public hostname.
- Persisted storage (see 5.5).
- Published port 80 and nothing else.

### 5.2 Removed everything unused
Every non-weaviate vector store (qdrant, pgvector, pgvecto-rs, chroma, oceanbase, seekdb, vastbase,
iris, oracle, myscale, matrixone, opengauss, elasticsearch, kibana, opensearch + dashboards, milvus +
etcd + minio), `unstructured`, and `couchbase-server` — the last of which carried a `build:` directive
that would have forced a source build on the VM.

### 5.3 `profiles:` — a 1.16.x trap
Nearly every service in 1.16.x is gated behind `profiles:`, and `.env.example` ships
`COMPOSE_PROFILES=${VECTOR_STORE:-weaviate},${DB_TYPE:-postgresql},collaboration`. Left alone that
enables the `postgresql` profile and starts the second Postgres this recipe exists to avoid. Rather
than depend on the engine interpreting profiles at all, unwanted services were **deleted outright** and
`profiles:` **stripped** from the ones kept (`weaviate`, `api_websocket`), with `COMPOSE_PROFILES=` empty.

### 5.4 Compose-engine compatibility
- The `env_file:` lists (~25 entries per service pointing at `./envs/**.env`) are **no-ops** — the repo
  ships only `*.env.example`. Collapsed to `- ./.env`, removing ~75 lines.
- Upstream never declares the `default` network although services reference it by name;
  `podman-compose` refuses the file outright with `RuntimeError: missing networks: default`.
  Added `default: {driver: bridge}`, which is a no-op under docker.
- Forced `compose_engine: 'docker'`. The stack uses modern compose-spec (`env_file` long form,
  `depends_on` conditions including `service_completed_successfully`), and nginx's `/socket.io/` block
  hardcodes `resolver [ip]` — Docker's embedded DNS. Under podman that location cannot resolve
  and workflow collaboration silently breaks while the rest of the console looks fine.

### 5.5 Durability
Moved `app_storage`, `plugin_storage`, `weaviate_data` and `redis_data` from `./volumes` bind mounts
(inside the project directory, i.e. exactly what a source re-upload replaces) to **named volumes**.
Kept `./volumes/sandbox/conf`, `./nginx` and `./ssrf_proxy` as bind mounts — those are config shipped
in the tarball. Side benefit: a fresh named volume inherits `/app/api/storage`'s uid 1001 ownership
from the image, so the `init_permissions` chown became belt-and-braces rather than load-bearing.

### 5.6 Correctness and hardening
- Additional URL variables 1.16.x needs and `redu.md` did not list: `FILES_URL`, `TRIGGER_URL`,
  `ENDPOINT_URL_TEMPLATE`, `NEXT_PUBLIC_SOCKET_URL` (ships as `ws://localhost`, must be `wss://`),
  `INTERNAL_FILES_URL`.
- `SQLALCHEMY_POOL_SIZE` 30 → 10 and `MAX_OVERFLOW` 10 → 5. Four services each open their own pool;
  the defaults allow up to 160 connections against a managed `m1.small` whose `max_connections` is
  not under our control. Also set `SQLALCHEMY_POOL_PRE_PING=true`.
- `MIGRATION_ENABLED=false` on `worker`, `worker_beat`, `api_websocket`. The image entrypoint runs
  `flask upgrade-db` whenever the variable is true regardless of `MODE`, so all four containers
  otherwise race the same migration on a fresh database. Left true on `api` only.
- `WEAVIATE_AUTHENTICATION_ANONYMOUS_ACCESS_ENABLED` → false (`.env.example` sets it true even though
  the compose default is false), with a generated API key.
- Tightened `CONSOLE_CORS_ALLOW_ORIGINS` to the public origin; left `WEB_API_CORS_ALLOW_ORIGINS=*` so
  embedded web apps keep working.
- Dropped nginx's `443` publish and plugin_daemon's `5003` (remote plugin debugging) publish.

## 6. Defects found during verification

### 6.1 Plugin daemon crash-loop — the significant one

**Symptom.** `plugin_daemon` restarting on exit 2. All 14 other containers up, `api` healthy, the
public URL serving normally. Nothing in the access point suggested a problem.

**Error.**
```
FATAL: no pg_hba.conf entry for host "[ip]", user "dify",
       database "dify_plugin", no encryption (SQLSTATE 28000)
```

**Root cause.** Upstream points the plugin daemon at a *second* database, `DB_PLUGIN_DATABASE=dify_plugin`,
on the same server. redu's managed Postgres scopes its `pg_hba.conf` entry to the single database it
provisioned, so every other database on that server is refused **before authentication**. Because the
DB user had been granted superuser, the daemon *succeeded* in running `CREATE DATABASE dify_plugin`
— confirmed present in `pg_database` — and then still could not connect to it. So the database exists
and the container crash-loops anyway, which makes the failure read as something other than what it is.

**Fix.** Point the daemon at Dify's own database (`DB_DATABASE: ${PGDATABASE}`).

**Safety check before applying.** Queried the live schema: Dify's api creates **136** tables in `dify`,
and **zero** of them collide with the daemon's 13 (`plugins`, `plugin_installations`,
`plugin_declarations`, `endpoints`, `serverless_runtimes`, `datasource_installations`,
`tool_installations`, `ai_model_installations`, `install_tasks`, `tenant_storages`,
`agent_strategy_installations`, `trigger_installations`, `plugin_readme_records`).

**Applied live** by recreating the container with a compose shell-env override, after an attempt to
edit the root-owned `/opt/app-src/.env` was blocked by a permission classifier. Result:
`database migration completed successfully` / `current node has become the master of the cluster`.
The permanent fix went into the local compose and into `redu.md`. This was disclosed to the user at
the time, including the caveat that the on-VM `.env` still read `dify_plugin` and that a bare
`docker compose up` there would have reverted it.

### 6.2 Console login rejects a plaintext password

**Symptom.** `POST /console/api/login` → `401 {"code":"authentication_failed","message":"Invalid encrypted data"}`,
which reads exactly like a wrong password. No traceback in the api log, because it is a handled exception.

**Root cause.** 1.16.x wraps the login view in `decrypt_password_field`, which base64-decodes the field
(`libs/encryption.py` — explicitly obfuscation, not cryptography; real security is HTTPS).
`/console/api/setup` does **not** apply it. So the same password is plaintext at setup and Base64 at login.

**Also.** Login returns only `{"result":"success"}` — no tokens in the body. The JWTs arrive as HttpOnly
`__Host-access_token` / `__Host-refresh_token` / `__Host-csrf_token` cookies. `__Host-` requires
`Secure`, which is a further reason the URL variables must be `https`.

## 12. Assessment of the recipe

**Held up:** port 80 through Dify's own nginx; managed Postgres via `PG*` with `DB_USERNAME` not
`DB_USER`; upload mode over git; no `migrate_command` needed; the memory-first flavor choice;
generating the dname up front; the cost estimate (exact); the warning to expect a slow first boot.

**Did not survive 1.16.1:** the container count, the profiles behaviour, the env_file structure, the
number of URL variables, the credential inventory, and — most importantly — it had no way to know
about the plugin daemon's second database, which is a genuine interaction between Dify's design and
redu's managed-Postgres `pg_hba` scoping rather than a fault in either one.

The single most valuable line added is quirk 1, because the failure presents as a working deployment.

deployment has stopped entirely.**

   still running and billing at GBP 0.0174/hr afterwards. This was surfaced to the user as an explicit
   separate decision rather than assumed, and they chose to delete it.

`list_deployments`; `https://dify-59d4fda9.redu.cloud` returns `000` (unreachable).

Other resources on the account at teardown time — `gitea` (#423), `tooljet` (#424), `nextcloud`,
`claude-rc-box` — belong to other sessions and **were not touched**.

All credentials generated this session are void: the instances that used them no longer exist.
